optical-design-001.question: In an optical system made of several lenses, the stop that limits the width of the light bundle from an on-axis object point is called the aperture stop. Which correctly describes the “entrance pupil”?
choices: The image of the aperture stop seen from the object side through the lenses in front of it
The stop that limits the light reaching the edge of the image plane and so determines the size of the field of view
The rim of the lens closest to the object in the optical system itself, whose diameter is the entrance pupil diameter
optical-design-001.explanation: The entrance pupil is the object-side image of the aperture stop: the apparent opening through which light enters as seen from the object side. The angle the entrance pupil subtends at the object point sets the object-side numerical aperture, and for an object at infinity the focal length divided by the entrance-pupil diameter is the f-number (f/D). Likewise, the image-side image of the aperture stop is the exit pupil. What determines the field of view is not the aperture stop but the field stop, which the option describing a stop that determines the field of view confuses with it. The rim of the front lens is the entrance pupil only if it is itself the aperture stop; in many camera lenses, the entrance pupil is the image of a stop smaller than the front element. The chief ray is defined as the ray through the center of the entrance pupil.

optical-design-002.question: A camera lens is stopped down from f/2.8 to f/4. For an object at infinity, by roughly what factor does the image-plane irradiance change? (Assume irradiance is proportional to the entrance-pupil area and inversely proportional to the square of the focal length.)
choices: About 0.71 times
About 0.25 times
About 0.49 times (about 1/2)
optical-design-002.explanation: The f-number is N = f/D (D is the entrance-pupil diameter). Image-plane irradiance is proportional to the pupil area D² and inversely proportional to the square of the focal length f, which sets the image size, so E ∝ (D/f)² = 1/N². Therefore (2.8/4)² ≈ 0.49, about 1/2. The f-number series 1.4, 2, 2.8, 4, 5.6 steps by √2 so that each full stop halves the light exactly. About 0.71 times takes the f-number ratio 2.8/4 directly as the irradiance ratio, and about 0.25 times is the value for stopping down two stops (f/2.8 → f/5.6). Doubling the exposure time restores the same exposure.

optical-design-003.question: Which of the following is not one of the third-order aberrations (the five Seidel aberrations) that arise in monochromatic light when rays depart from the paraxial regime?
choices: Comatic aberration
Axial chromatic aberration
Distortion
optical-design-003.explanation: The five Seidel aberrations are spherical aberration, coma, astigmatism, field curvature and distortion: monochromatic aberrations that arise when a lens's aperture or field angle grows and the paraxial approximation sinθ ≈ θ no longer holds. Because they appear as third-order terms in ray height and field angle, they are also called third-order aberrations. Chromatic aberration arises because the refractive index varies with wavelength (dispersion) and does not appear in monochromatic light, so it is treated separately from the five Seidel aberrations. Chromatic aberration comes in two forms: axial chromatic aberration, in which the focal position shifts with wavelength, and lateral chromatic aberration, in which the magnification shifts. Coma and distortion are both monochromatic aberrations that appear for off-axis object points and belong to the five.

optical-design-004.question: Which correctly describes distortion?
choices: It does not blur point images but changes magnification with field angle; in barrel distortion, magnification decreases toward the edge of the image
It blurs point images and is reduced by stopping down to narrow the light bundle
In pincushion distortion, magnification decreases toward the edge of the image, and in barrel distortion it increases
optical-design-004.explanation: Distortion keeps points imaged as points but shifts image positions from their ideal locations. Because magnification changes with field angle (image height), straight lines are imaged as curves. If magnification decreases toward the edge, the sides of a square grid bulge outward — barrel distortion; if it increases, they bow inward — pincushion distortion. The option saying that magnification decreases toward the edge in pincushion distortion reverses these directions. Because distortion is set by the path of the chief ray rather than by blur, stopping down to narrow the bundle does not reduce it. It is easy to cancel with a configuration that is symmetric about the stop and can also be corrected afterward by image processing. In dimensional measurement, even slight distortion becomes a measurement error.

optical-design-005.question: With a lens that images points well on the optical axis, the image of an off-axis point source takes the shape of a comet with a tail extending in one direction. Which aberration is mainly responsible for this image shape?
choices: Spherical aberration
Coma
Distortion
optical-design-005.explanation: Coma arises for off-axis object points: rays passing through different annular zones of the pupil are imaged at different magnifications, so the image takes the shape of a comet with a head and tail. Its size is proportional to the square of the aperture and to the field angle, so it is more conspicuous off-axis and at large apertures. A design that satisfies the sine condition (an aplanatic design) corrects coma along with spherical aberration. Spherical aberration occurs on-axis as well, and its image is a blur (halo) symmetric about the optical axis, so it does not fit the condition “good on-axis, asymmetric off-axis”. Distortion only shifts the image position without blurring the shape of a point image, so it does not fit either.

optical-design-006.question: In an optical system with astigmatism, how does the image of an off-axis point source look as the focus is changed?
choices: The image is a circular blur symmetric about the optical axis that only changes size as focus is moved, never becoming line-shaped
Each point is imaged to a single point, but the surface of best focus is a curved surface set by the Petzval sum, so the edges of a flat sensor blur
Meridional and sagittal rays focus at different positions, giving two perpendicular line images with the circle of least confusion between them
optical-design-006.explanation: Astigmatism is an aberration in which, for the light bundle from an off-axis object point, the rays in the plane containing the object point and the optical axis (the meridional plane) and those in the plane perpendicular to it (the sagittal plane) focus at different positions. Moving the focus, you see first a line image stretched in one direction, then a nearly circular circle of least confusion, and further on a line image rotated by 90°. Astigmatism of the eye has the same character. When each point is imaged to a single point but the surface of best focus is curved, that is field curvature, a different aberration (governed by the Petzval sum). A circular blur symmetric about the axis is characteristic of on-axis spherical aberration.

optical-design-007.question: An achromatic lens (achromat) with a combined focal length of 100 mm is made by cementing a convex lens of crown glass (Abbe number V₁ = 64) to a concave lens of flint glass (Abbe number V₂ = 36). Using the condition for bringing two wavelengths to the same focus, φ₁/V₁ + φ₂/V₂ = 0 (φ is optical power = 1/f), which pair of focal lengths is closest? (Treat them as thin lenses.)
choices: Convex lens about 43.8 mm, concave lens about −77.8 mm
Convex lens about 77.8 mm, concave lens about −43.8 mm
Convex lens about 50 mm, concave lens about −100 mm
optical-design-007.explanation: Solving the combined power φ₁ + φ₂ = 1/100 mm⁻¹ together with the achromatic condition gives φ₁ = φV₁/(V₁ − V₂) = 0.01 × 64/28 ≈ 0.0229 mm⁻¹ and φ₂ = −φV₂/(V₁ − V₂) ≈ −0.0129 mm⁻¹, so f₁ ≈ 43.8 mm and f₂ ≈ −77.8 mm. The low-dispersion crown (high Abbe number) carries strong positive power and the high-dispersion flint carries weak negative power, so that only the color error cancels. With the two focal lengths swapped (about 77.8 mm and about −43.8 mm), the concave lens is stronger, making the combination a negative lens. About 50 mm and about −100 mm satisfy only the combined focal length, not the achromatic condition. The larger the difference in Abbe numbers, the weaker each element's power can be, which also makes other aberrations easier to control.

optical-design-008.question: Two luminous points (incoherent point sources) emitting at 500 nm are observed with an aberration-free microscope objective with a numerical aperture NA = 0.95. Which value is closest to the minimum separation that can be resolved by the Rayleigh criterion (the center of one point image falls on the first dark ring of the other)?
choices: About 0.26 µm
About 0.64 µm
About 0.32 µm
optical-design-008.explanation: The radius of the first dark ring of the point image (Airy pattern) of a circular aperture is 0.61λ/NA in object-side dimensions. The Rayleigh criterion takes the limit of resolution as the separation equal to this, so d = 0.61 × 0.5 µm / 0.95 ≈ 0.32 µm. About 0.26 µm is λ/(2NA), the limit for resolving a periodic structure with oblique illumination (Abbe's formula), which rests on different assumptions from the Rayleigh criterion for two incoherent points. About 0.64 µm wrongly carries the factor 1.22 from the angular formula 1.22λ/D into the numerical-aperture formula (D is a diameter, so converting to the half-angle sinθ gives 0.61). Resolution is improved by shortening the wavelength or by raising NA, for example with oil immersion.

optical-design-009.question: An object under incoherent illumination at 0.55 µm is photographed with an aberration-free lens at f/4. Which value is closest to the diffraction-determined MTF cutoff spatial frequency (the frequency at which the MTF reaches zero in the image plane)?
choices: About 227 cycles/mm
About 455 cycles/mm
About 909 cycles/mm
optical-design-009.explanation: In incoherent imaging, the MTF of an aberration-free system with a circular aperture falls smoothly with spatial frequency and reaches zero at the cutoff frequency fc = 1/(λN) = 2NA/λ (the image-side NA is about 1/(2N)). fc = 1/(0.55×10⁻³ mm × 4) ≈ 455 cycles/mm. About 227 cycles/mm is 1/(2λN) = NA/λ, the cutoff for the same lens under coherent illumination. In incoherent imaging the OTF is the autocorrelation of the pupil function, so the cutoff is twice the coherent value. About 909 cycles/mm doubles the factor once more. In practice the frequencies limited by aberrations or pixels are usually lower, and fc serves as a rough upper bound on performance.

optical-design-010.question: A high-performance lens that retains ample MTF at spatial frequencies finer than the pixel pitch is paired with an image sensor with a 3.0 µm pixel pitch. When a subject with fine stripes is photographed, which correctly pairs the likely phenomenon with its countermeasure?
choices: Aberrations lower the contrast of the whole image uniformly, so the fix is to open up the lens aperture and push the cutoff frequency higher
Components above the Nyquist frequency alias to lower frequencies as moiré, so an optical low-pass filter attenuates the high frequencies
Components above the Nyquist frequency are averaged out by the pixel apertures and removed by the sensor, so no false stripes or colors appear
optical-design-010.explanation: The highest spatial frequency an image sensor with pixel pitch p can represent is the Nyquist frequency 1/(2p): for 3.0 µm, 1/(2 × 0.003 mm) ≈ 167 cycles/mm. If the lens delivers components at higher frequencies to the image plane, sampling folds them back to lower frequencies (aliasing), and they appear as stripes and false color (moiré) that are not in the subject. After sampling they cannot be distinguished from real stripes, so the countermeasure is to place an optical low-pass filter, such as a birefringent plate, in front of the sensor to attenuate the high frequencies optically. Averaging over the pixel aperture alone does not eliminate aliasing, so the option claiming that the sensor removes these components automatically is wrong. A uniform loss of contrast is a symptom of aberrations or flare, and opening the aperture raises the cutoff, which actually increases aliasing.

optical-design-011.question: Which correctly describes the MTF (modulation transfer function) used to express the performance of an optical system?
choices: It expresses the amount of image distortion as a function of field angle, showing by what percentage image points shift at the edge
For an aberration-free, diffraction-limited system, it stays flat at 1 from zero spatial frequency up to the cutoff and then drops abruptly to zero
It expresses the ratio of image to object contrast for a sinusoidal object as a function of spatial frequency, equal to the magnitude of the Fourier transform of the PSF
optical-design-011.explanation: The MTF describes how much of the contrast (Imax − Imin)/(Imax + Imin) of a sinusoidal pattern at spatial frequency ν is preserved in the image. In incoherent imaging the image is the convolution of the object with the PSF, so the magnitude of the optical transfer function (OTF), the Fourier transform of the PSF, is the MTF, and its phase is the PTF. Even for a diffraction-limited circular aperture, the MTF falls smoothly from 1 at zero frequency to zero at the cutoff, so the option describing a flat response at 1 up to the cutoff is wrong (a flat shape is characteristic of the coherent transfer function). Distortion shifts image positions without reducing contrast, so it cannot be evaluated with the MTF and is expressed separately as a distortion percentage. The MTF of a whole system, such as a lens plus image sensor, is normally estimated as the product of the MTFs of its elements.

optical-design-012.question: A 50 mm lens is stopped down to f/8, with an acceptable circle of confusion of 0.03 mm diameter. Which pair is closest to the hyperfocal distance H ≈ f²/(Nc) and the near limit of the depth of field when focused there?
choices: Hyperfocal distance about 10.4 m; near limit about 5.2 m (sharp out to infinity)
Hyperfocal distance about 10.4 m; near limit also about 10.4 m (anything closer is blurred)
Hyperfocal distance about 5.2 m; near limit about 2.6 m
optical-design-012.explanation: H ≈ f²/(Nc) = 50² / (8 × 0.03) ≈ 10400 mm, or about 10.4 m. H is the nearest distance imaged within the acceptable circle of confusion when focused at infinity; conversely, focusing at H extends the depth of field from H/2 ≈ 5.2 m to infinity. The exact formula H = f²/(Nc) + f gives about 10.47 m, which does not change the conclusion. A near limit of about 10.4 m confuses this with the near limit when focused at infinity. About 5.2 m and about 2.6 m put an extra factor of 2 in the denominator. Depth of field increases with stopping down and, at the same shooting distance, with shorter focal length. The acceptable circle of confusion is a conventional value chosen for the viewing conditions.

optical-design-013.question: In a diffraction-limited imaging system, the numerical aperture NA is doubled (at the same wavelength). Which correctly pairs the change in the minimum resolvable lateral separation and in the depth of focus (taken as proportional to λ/NA²)?
choices: The resolvable separation halves, and the depth of focus also halves
The resolvable separation halves, and the depth of focus falls to 1/4
The resolvable separation falls to 1/4, and the depth of focus halves
optical-design-013.explanation: The resolvable lateral separation is inversely proportional to NA, as in 0.61λ/NA, so doubling NA halves it. The depth of focus, however, is inversely proportional to NA squared, as in ±λ/(2NA²), so it shrinks to 1/2² = 1/4. With a larger focusing angle, the light bundle spreads out quickly when the focus is off. The option halving both misses the square dependence of the depth of focus, and the option giving 1/4 for the separation and 1/2 for the depth of focus swaps the two dependences. In semiconductor lithography, raising NA to improve resolution makes the depth of focus sharply shallower, tightening the requirements on wafer flatness and focus accuracy.

optical-design-014.question: The root-mean-square (RMS) wavefront aberration of an optical system is λ/14. Which value is closest to the Strehl ratio given by the Maréchal approximation S ≈ exp[−(2πσ/λ)²] (σ is the RMS wavefront aberration)?
choices: About 0.64
About 0.99
About 0.82
optical-design-014.explanation: (2πσ/λ)² = (2π/14)² ≈ 0.201, so S ≈ exp(−0.201) ≈ 0.82. The Strehl ratio is the peak intensity of the point image of the aberrated system divided by that of an aberration-free, diffraction-limited system. Because an RMS wavefront aberration of λ/14 gives S ≈ 0.8, “RMS ≤ λ/14, S ≥ 0.8” is used as a practical benchmark for diffraction-limited performance (the Maréchal criterion). About 0.99 forgets the 2π and puts (1/14)² in the exponent, and about 0.64 forgets the square and uses exp(−2π/14). Note also that wavefront aberration is an optical path error, so for a reflecting mirror the wavefront error is twice the surface figure error.

optical-design-015.question: A plano-convex lens focuses a collimated beam to a spot. Which orientation of the lens reduces spherical aberration?
choices: Curved (convex) side toward the collimated beam, flat side toward the focus
Flat side toward the collimated beam, curved side toward the focus
It is a thin lens, so changing its orientation does not change spherical aberration
optical-design-015.explanation: Spherical aberration grows the more the ray bending is concentrated at one surface. With the convex side toward the collimated beam, the refraction is shared between the convex and flat surfaces (roughly 2:1 for n = 1.5), so aberration is smaller. With the flat side toward the collimated beam, the flat surface does no bending at all and the convex surface alone must bend the rays strongly, increasing longitudinal spherical aberration about fourfold (for n = 1.5). A basic point of lens design is that, for the same focal length, aberration changes with how the curvature is distributed between the two surfaces (lens bending); even in the thin-lens approximation, third-order spherical aberration depends on shape, so orientation is not irrelevant. When collimating light from a point source, the convex side also faces the collimated beam. To reduce aberration further, aspheric lenses or multi-element combinations are used.

optical-design-016.question: With a camera lens, the edges of the frame sometimes darken when the aperture is wide open and improve when it is stopped down. Which is the main cause?
choices: Cosine-fourth falloff set by the field angle; stopping down increases the value of cos⁴θ, so the edges become brighter
Vignetting, in which part of an oblique bundle is blocked by lens mounts and similar edges; stopping down narrows the bundle so less is blocked
Distortion, which grows toward the edges of the frame; stopping down reduces the distortion and evens out the image brightness across the whole frame
optical-design-016.explanation: An oblique bundle from an off-axis point may pass through the aperture stop yet still be partly clipped by lens mounts or a hood in front of or behind the stop, reducing the light reaching the image. This is vignetting, and the cross-section of the bundle has a portion cut away. Stopping down restricts the bundle at the stop so that it no longer strikes those edges, and the corner darkening improves. Cosine-fourth falloff depends only on the ray angle and does not change when stopping down. Distortion shifts image positions, does not change with the stop and does not darken the edges.

optical-design-017.question: An aberration-free lens without vignetting images a surface of uniform brightness. At the point of the image where the image-side bundle travels at 30° to the axis, the irradiance is roughly what percentage of the on-axis irradiance? Assume the cosine-fourth law.
choices: About 56%
About 87%
About 75%
optical-design-017.explanation: cos⁴30° = (0.866)⁴ ≈ 0.5625, so about 56%. Two of the four cosine factors come from the longer oblique distance between the image point and the pupil, since irradiance falls as the inverse square of distance; one comes from the reduced apparent area of the pupil seen obliquely; and the last comes from light striking the image plane obliquely, spreading over more area. About 87% includes cosθ only once, and about 75% includes only cos²θ. This is why wide-angle lenses tend to darken at the edges, and designers preserve edge illumination by placing the exit pupil carefully or making the image side closer to telecentric.

optical-design-018.question: Field curvature, which tends to remain even in an otherwise corrected lens system, is set by the Petzval sum Σ 1/(nᵢfᵢ), where nᵢ and fᵢ are the index and focal length of each lens. Which is a correct way to flatten the image field?
choices: Change the bending of the positive lens (how curvature is shared between its surfaces) to make the Petzval sum zero while keeping its focal length
Stop down the aperture to narrow the bundle, bringing the Petzval sum close to zero and flattening the field
Use high-index glass for the positive lenses and combine them with a separated negative lens, reducing the Petzval sum while keeping the system's power
optical-design-018.explanation: The Petzval sum depends only on the power and index of each lens, not on lens bending or on the position or size of the stop. A system of positive lenses alone leaves a positive sum and a curved field. To reduce it, negative lenses are added, with high-index glass for the positive lenses and low-index glass for the negative ones. Placing the negative lens apart, where the ray height differs, cancels the Petzval sum without costing much of the system's total power. Stopping down deepens the depth of focus so the curvature is less noticeable, but the sum itself does not change.

optical-design-019.question: Why can a single aspheric lens focus a collimated laser beam to a nearly diffraction-limited spot?
choices: Its surface departs slightly from a sphere so that rays near the edge are bent less, bringing all rays to a single point
In an asphere the refractive index varies continuously from the center to the edge of the lens, eliminating the wavelength-dependent focus shift (chromatic aberration)
Making the surface aspheric lowers the numerical aperture and enlarges the Airy disk, so blur from aberrations becomes less noticeable
optical-design-019.explanation: In a spherical lens, rays near the edge are bent too strongly and focus short of the paraxial focus, producing spherical aberration. An aspheric lens varies the surface slope with height from the axis, bending edge rays less, so the optical path lengths of all rays to the focus are equalized, and a single element can nearly eliminate on-axis spherical aberration for monochromatic light. A lens whose index varies with position is a GRIN lens; an asphere changes only the shape. The material's dispersion is unchanged, so chromatic aberration remains. Lowering the numerical aperture to hide aberrations would reduce resolution and is not the purpose of an asphere.

optical-design-020.question: A subject is photographed at life size (lateral magnification −1) with an F/4 lens. Which pair correctly gives the working f-number N_w ≈ N(1 + |m|), where m is the lateral magnification, and the image-plane irradiance compared with photographing an object at infinity?
choices: The working f-number stays at 4, and the image irradiance is unchanged
The working f-number is 8, and the image irradiance falls to about 1/4
The working f-number is 5.6, and the image irradiance falls to about 1/2
optical-design-020.explanation: At life size the image distance is twice the focal length, so the cone of light seen from the image side is narrower than for an object at infinity, and the working f-number is N(1 + |m|) = 4 × 2 = 8. Image irradiance is inversely proportional to the square of the working f-number, so it drops to (4/8)² = 1/4, requiring two stops more exposure. The marked f-number applies when focused at infinity, so assuming the irradiance is unchanged at close range is wrong. 5.6 corresponds to only one stop of darkening, counting just half the effect of doubling the image distance. The diffraction blur is also set by the working f-number, so diffraction matters more in close-up photography.

optical-design-021.question: In an f-theta lens used for scanning in laser processing or laser printers, the focal length is 100 mm and the scan angle of the galvanometer mirror (the angle from the optical axis) is ±30°. Which value is closest to the total scan length on the image plane?
choices: About 115 mm
About 100 mm
About 105 mm
optical-design-021.explanation: An f-theta lens is given deliberate distortion so that the image height is h = fθ (θ in radians), so h = 100 × (π/6) ≈ 52.4 mm and the total length is about 105 mm. About 115 mm is calculated with the image height of an ordinary lens, h = f tanθ (100 × tan30° ≈ 57.7 mm), and about 100 mm uses h = f sinθ. With an f tanθ lens, even when the mirror swings at a constant angular velocity, the spot moves faster toward the edges and the spacing of the dots widens. With an f-theta lens the scan speed on the image plane is constant, so pulses emitted at fixed intervals write equally spaced dots.

optical-design-022.question: A telescope with a 60 mm objective aperture and a magnification of 20 is used at night by an eye whose pupil is about 7 mm in diameter. Which correctly describes the exit-pupil diameter and the image brightness?
choices: The exit pupil is 60/20 = 3 mm across, smaller than the eye's pupil, so all the light entering the objective reaches the eye
The exit pupil is 60 mm across, the same as the objective, and larger than the eye's pupil, so most of the light does not reach the eye
The exit pupil is 60 × 20 = 1200 mm across, and raising the magnification enlarges the exit pupil and brightens the image
optical-design-022.explanation: The exit pupil of a telescope is the image of the objective, which serves as the aperture stop, formed by the eyepiece; its diameter is aperture/magnification = 60/20 = 3 mm. With the eye placed there, all the light entering the objective passes through this 3 mm, fits within the 7 mm pupil and reaches the eye without waste. Conversely, if the exit pupil were larger than the eye's pupil, the light outside would be wasted. Raising the magnification for the same aperture makes the exit pupil smaller and reduces the surface brightness of the magnified image. Taking the exit pupil to be the same size as the objective forgets the imaging by the eyepiece. Multiplying by the magnification is also backward; the exit-pupil diameter is inversely proportional to the magnification.

optical-design-023.question: Which correctly describes the function of the field stop in an optical system?
choices: It limits the width of the light bundle from an on-axis object point and sets the image brightness and the diffraction-limited resolution
It is placed at the object or image plane (or a conjugate plane) and sharply defines the boundary of the imaged region (the field of view)
It absorbs light reflected from lens surfaces, reducing ghosts and flare and raising the image contrast
optical-design-023.explanation: A field stop is placed at a position conjugate to the image, such as the object plane or an intermediate image plane, so its edge appears sharply as the boundary of the field and determines how much of the scene is imaged. Examples are the circular frame at the focal plane of a telescope or microscope eyepiece and the frame of the image sensor itself. The stop that limits the width of the on-axis bundle and sets the brightness (f-number or NA) and the resolution is the aperture stop, which lies at a position conjugate to the pupils. Stops that reduce reflections and stray light are called baffles or flare stops and serve a different purpose from the field stop. The key distinction is that the aperture stop is conjugate to the pupils and the field stop is conjugate to the image.

optical-design-024.question: Why can a diffractive optical element (a diffractive lens) be combined with a refractive lens to correct chromatic aberration?
choices: A diffractive lens bends longer wavelengths more strongly, with an equivalent Abbe number of about −3.5, negative and small in magnitude, so a weak diffractive lens can cancel chromatic aberration
A diffractive lens has the same focal length at every wavelength, so combining it with a refractive lens dilutes the refractive lens's chromatic aberration by half
A diffractive lens bends shorter wavelengths more strongly and has a very large Abbe number of about 90, so it acts as a material with lower dispersion than glass
optical-design-024.explanation: The power of a diffractive lens is proportional to wavelength (its focal length is inversely proportional to wavelength), so it bends longer wavelengths more strongly. This is opposite to the normal dispersion of glass, and its equivalent Abbe number is V = λd/(λF − λC) = 587.6/(486.1 − 656.3) ≈ −3.45. Because its sign is opposite and its magnitude small, assigning just a small part of the total power to a diffractive lens cancels the chromatic aberration of a positive refractive lens, making the system lighter and thinner than an achromat that uses a negative flint element. Diffraction depends strongly on wavelength, so the claim that the focal length is independent of wavelength is wrong. A large Abbe number and low dispersion belong to materials such as fluorite, the opposite of a diffractive lens.

optical-design-025.question: In an achromat (an achromatic doublet of two cemented glasses), the foci for the F line (486 nm) and the C line (656 nm) are made to coincide, yet some chromatic aberration (secondary spectrum) remains. Which correctly gives this residual and the way to reduce it further?
choices: Secondary spectrum is a kind of spherical aberration determined by surface shape rather than color, so it disappears if the lens surfaces are made aspheric
Secondary spectrum is determined by the difference in Abbe numbers, so it vanishes completely with the glass pair having the largest Abbe-number difference
It is a residual focus shift at other wavelengths, reduced in an apochromat using fluorite or ED glass with anomalous partial dispersion
optical-design-025.explanation: An achromat brings two wavelengths to a common focus, but for ordinary glasses the curvature of the index-versus-wavelength curve (the partial dispersion ratio) lies on nearly the same straight line against the Abbe number, so the foci for wavelengths between and beyond those two remain slightly shifted. This is the secondary spectrum. Combining fluorite or ED (anomalous partial dispersion) glass, whose partial dispersion departs from this line, brings three wavelengths to a common focus, giving an apochromat. Secondary spectrum is a chromatic aberration that does not occur in monochromatic light, so making the surfaces aspheric cannot correct it. A larger Abbe-number difference lets each element have less power and reduces the secondary spectrum somewhat, but it does not vanish as long as the partial dispersion ratios follow the same line.

optical-design-026.question: A thin singlet lens of N-BK7 (Abbe number Vd = 64.17) has a focal length of 100 mm. Which value is closest to the difference between the focal positions for the F line (486 nm) and the C line (656 nm) (axial chromatic aberration, Δf ≈ f/Vd)?
choices: About 1.6 mm
About 0.81 mm
About 0.16 mm
optical-design-026.explanation: The power of a thin lens is proportional to (n − 1), so the difference in power between the F and C lines is φ(nF − nC)/(nd − 1) = φ/Vd. The focal shift is therefore Δf ≈ f/Vd = 100 mm / 64.17 ≈ 1.56 mm, about 1.6 mm, with the blue F-line focus, where the index is higher, closer to the lens. About 0.81 mm is f × (nF − nC) = 100 × 0.0081, forgetting to divide by (nd − 1). About 0.16 mm gets the power of ten wrong. The depth of focus of an f/4 lens is a few tens of µm, so a 1.6 mm color shift shows up strongly as color fringing and must be corrected with an achromat combining glasses of different Abbe numbers.

optical-design-027.question: A lens with a focal length of 50 mm (no distortion) is used with an image sensor 36 mm wide and 24 mm high to photograph a distant scene. Which value is closest to the horizontal angle of view (full angle)? (Angle of view = 2 arctan(w/(2f)), where w is the sensor width.)
choices: About 72°
About 47°
About 40°
optical-design-027.explanation: 2 arctan(36/(2 × 50)) = 2 arctan(0.36) ≈ 2 × 19.8° = 39.6°, about 40°. An object at infinity is imaged in the focal plane, and the chief ray reaching the edge of the sensor makes an angle arctan(18/50) with the axis, so the full angle is twice that. About 72° uses the full width of 36 mm instead of half of it, and about 47° is the angle of view across the diagonal (about 43.3 mm). The angle of view narrows as the focal length increases: with a 100 mm lens on the same sensor the horizontal angle is about 20°. A smaller sensor gives a narrower angle with the same focal length, so the picture looks like a telephoto shot.

optical-design-028.question: In a symmetric lens, with the aperture stop in the middle and the lenses in front of and behind it arranged as mirror images, some aberrations cancel automatically when it is used at unit magnification. Which combination of aberrations cancels?
choices: Spherical aberration and axial color, because ray heights are equal on both sides of the stop, so the axial aberrations of the front and rear halves take opposite signs and cancel
Coma, distortion and lateral color, because off-axis rays are bent in opposite senses on the two sides of the stop and the aberrations take opposite signs
Astigmatism and field curvature, because a symmetric arrangement makes the Petzval sum zero, so the image surface becomes flat and both aberrations vanish
optical-design-028.explanation: When the arrangement in front of and behind the stop is symmetric, off-axis chief rays follow paths that are symmetric about the stop center. Coma, distortion and lateral color have odd symmetry with respect to the stop: the front and rear halves contribute equal amounts of opposite sign, so they cancel at unit magnification. Spherical aberration and axial color are even and add with the same sign on both sides, so they do not cancel. The Petzval sum depends only on the powers and indices of the lenses, not on their arrangement, so symmetry does not make it zero, and astigmatism and field curvature are not removed automatically either. This is why many photographic lenses, such as the double-Gauss type, are nearly symmetric.

optical-design-029.question: In lens-design software, the ray-traced spot diagram (the geometric spot diameter) has become much smaller than the diameter of the Airy disk. Which assessment of this system's image is correct?
choices: The blur is set mainly by diffraction, so the system is diffraction limited, and reducing aberrations further cannot make the point image smaller than the Airy disk
Because the spot is smaller than the Airy disk, the point-image size is set by the geometric spot, and a resolution beyond the diffraction limit of the aperture is obtained
The smaller the spot, the stronger the diffraction, so the Airy disk grows even larger and the image actually becomes more blurred
optical-design-029.explanation: A ray-traced spot diagram contains no wave effects, so it indicates the size of the aberrations but does not necessarily show the actual size of the point image. When the geometric spot is much smaller than the Airy disk (diameter 2.44λN), the wavefront aberration is also small and the spread of the point image is set by diffraction at the aperture. In this regime performance is judged with measures that include diffraction, such as the MTF, the point spread function and the Strehl ratio. Reducing aberrations further does not make the point image smaller than the Airy disk. The diffraction spread is set by the aperture size and the wavelength, and does not grow stronger because the ray spot is small.

optical-design-030.question: Red and blue color fringes appear along the edges of white objects near the edge of the frame, and stopping down the lens hardly reduces them. Which aberration is the likely cause?
choices: Axial chromatic aberration: focus shifts along the axis with color, so the deeper depth of focus from stopping down leaves the shift unchanged
Lateral chromatic aberration: the image magnification differs with color and image points shift sideways, so the shift remains even with a narrower beam
Spherical aberration: edge rays separate the colors more strongly, so blocking them by stopping down leaves the color shift unchanged
optical-design-030.explanation: Lateral chromatic aberration is a difference in image magnification (image height) with wavelength; the chief ray itself lands at a sideways-shifted position for each color. Since the chief ray passes through the center of the stop, stopping down does not change the shift, which is zero at the center of the frame and grows toward the edges. Axial chromatic aberration is a shift of focus along the axis that also occurs at the center; stopping down narrows the beam and deepens the depth of focus, so the color blur shrinks. Spherical aberration occurs even with monochromatic light, does not separate colors, and decreases on stopping down. Lateral color can also be largely corrected in software by rescaling each color channel of the captured image.

optical-design-031.question: For a lens with distortion, the image height of a point in the corner of the frame is measured as 19.2 mm, whereas the paraxial image height without distortion would be 20.0 mm. Which combination of the distortion at this point (as a fraction of the paraxial image height) and its type is correct?
choices: About +4.0%, pincushion
About −0.8%, barrel
About −4.0%, barrel
optical-design-031.explanation: Distortion is expressed as (actual image height − paraxial image height)/paraxial image height, so (19.2 − 20.0)/20.0 = −0.04, about −4.0%. The peripheral image is pulled inward from its paraxial position, so the magnification decreases toward the edges: barrel distortion, in which a square grid is imaged bulging outward like a barrel. About +4.0% pincushion has the sign reversed and describes peripheral images pushed outward. About −0.8% reads the 0.8 mm difference in image height directly as a percentage. Because distortion does not blur point images, it can be corrected by image processing after capture, and barrel distortion of a few percent is common in wide-angle lenses. In dimensional measurement, whatever remains after this correction becomes measurement error.

optical-design-032.question: For incoherent imaging by an aberration-free lens with a circular aperture, which value is closest to the MTF at a spatial frequency exactly half the cutoff frequency νc? (MTF = (2/π)(φ − cosφ sinφ), with φ = arccos(ν/νc).)
choices: About 0.50
About 0.39
About 0.25
optical-design-032.explanation: At ν/νc = 0.5, φ = arccos0.5 = π/3 ≈ 1.047 rad and cosφ sinφ = 0.5 × 0.866 ≈ 0.433, so MTF = (2/π)(1.047 − 0.433) ≈ 0.39. The diffraction-limited MTF is given by the autocorrelation of the pupil (the overlap area of two shifted circles); it falls faster than a straight line from low frequencies and reaches 0 at the cutoff. About 0.50 assumes the MTF falls linearly with frequency, which is the case for a slit-like aperture with width in only one direction. About 0.25 multiplies that linear value of 0.5 for the horizontal and vertical directions; the MTF of a circular aperture is not a product of two directions. Aberrations lower the MTF further below this diffraction-limited value.

optical-design-033.question: If the lens in front of an image sensor is made image-side telecentric, the chief rays strike the image plane perpendicularly. Which property of such a lens is correct?
choices: The exit pupil is at infinity, so the image size hardly changes if the image plane shifts slightly, and light reaches the sensor perpendicularly even at the edges
The entrance pupil is at infinity, so the magnification does not change as the object moves along the axis, which suits measuring the dimensions of objects
The aperture stop is placed at the image plane, so the light bundles narrow toward the edge pixels and vignetting that darkens the edges is eliminated
optical-design-033.explanation: The chief ray passes through the center of the aperture stop, so the image-side chief rays are parallel to the axis when the exit pupil (the image of the stop seen from the image side) is at infinity. Since the chief rays meet the image plane perpendicularly, a slight shift of the image plane only blurs the image while leaving its position and size nearly unchanged. Microlenses, color filters and interference filters on the pixels also suffer less loss of sensitivity or color shift from oblique light at the edges. An entrance pupil at infinity is object-side telecentricity, and suppressing magnification changes with object position is that property. An aperture stop at the image plane could not limit the width of the light bundles and would not act as a stop. Making a lens image-side telecentric requires the last lens group to be at least as large as the image.

optical-design-034.question: A single-lens reflex camera needs room behind the lens for the moving mirror, so even a wide-angle lens may need a back focal distance (from the last lens surface to the image plane) longer than its focal length. Which lens configuration is used for this?
choices: A telephoto design with a positive group in front and a negative group behind, which moves the principal point forward and makes the overall length shorter than the focal length
A single thick positive group that moves the principal point forward, lengthening the back focal distance by the added thickness
A retrofocus design with a negative group in front and a positive group behind, which places the rear principal point behind the lens
optical-design-034.explanation: The focal length is measured from the rear principal point to the focus, so a back focal distance longer than the focal length requires the rear principal point to lie behind the last surface of the system (on the image side). In a retrofocus (inverted telephoto) design with a negative group in front and a positive group behind, the negative group spreads the light and the positive group then converges it, so the rear principal point moves behind the system and a long back focal distance is obtained even with a short focal length. The telephoto design, with a positive group in front and a negative group behind, does the opposite: it moves the principal point forward to make the overall length shorter than the focal length and is used for telephoto lenses. Thickening a positive group to move the principal point forward brings the focus closer to the lens and actually shortens the back focal distance.

optical-design-035.question: With a camera lens that retains some aberrations, stopping down from full aperture first improves the resolution at the center of the frame, and stopping down further makes it worse again. Which explanation of this behavior is correct?
choices: Stopping down makes the depth of field shallower and narrows the in-focus range, so beyond a certain aperture even the center image blurs
Stopping down reduces aberration blur, but diffraction blur grows in proportion to the f-number, so an optimum aperture lies in between
Stopping down lowers the image-plane illuminance and increases sensor noise, so resolution worsens once the light becomes insufficient
optical-design-035.explanation: Blur from aberrations such as spherical aberration shrinks rapidly as the aperture is reduced (the transverse blur from third-order spherical aberration is proportional to the cube of the aperture radius). The diameter of the diffraction Airy disk, 2.44λN, instead grows in proportion to the f-number N. Aberrations dominate near full aperture and diffraction dominates when stopped down far, so resolution is best at an intermediate aperture where the two balance. The better corrected the lens, the closer this optimum lies to full aperture. Stopping down deepens the depth of field, so the claim that it becomes shallower is backwards. Lower illuminance can be offset by a longer exposure to reduce noise, so it is not the main reason the resolution worsens.

optical-design-036.question: What property does a lens designed to satisfy Abbe's sine condition have? (For an object at infinity, the condition is that the ray height h and the image-side angle θ′ to the axis satisfy h = f sinθ′; spherical aberration is assumed to be corrected.)
choices: The image height is proportional to f tanθ at every field angle, so distortion vanishes and straight lines stay straight even at wide angles
The focal length is the same at all wavelengths, so both axial and lateral colour vanish and no colour fringing appears
Rays through every part of the aperture image with the same magnification, so off-axis points near the axis are free of coma
optical-design-036.explanation: Coma arises because rays through the centre and the edge of the aperture image an off-axis point with different magnifications. The sine condition gives the same focal length (magnification) to rays through every zone of the aperture; combined with correction of spherical aberration, it makes the system aplanatic, imaging sharply off-axis points near the axis. Making the image height equal to f tanθ is the condition for zero distortion and concerns the field angle, not the aperture. The sine condition is a monochromatic condition, so chromatic aberration must be corrected separately, for example by combining glasses with different Abbe numbers. The relation F ≈ 1/(2NA) between f-number and numerical aperture also assumes this condition.

optical-design-037.question: A lens with residual spherical aberration is stopped down from F2 to F4 without changing its focal length. By roughly what factor does the maximum transverse ray error due to spherical aberration (the transverse aberration), observed in the paraxial focal plane, change? (Consider third-order aberration only.)
choices: About 1/4
About 1/8
About 1/16
optical-design-037.explanation: For third-order spherical aberration, the transverse displacement in the paraxial focal plane of a ray passing at aperture radius h is proportional to h³. Stopping down from F2 to F4 halves h, so the transverse aberration becomes (1/2)³ = 1/8. About 1/4 confuses it with the longitudinal aberration, the shift of the ray's axis crossing, which is proportional to h²; the transverse aberration is the longitudinal aberration times the ray slope, which is proportional to h. About 1/16 applies the h⁴ dependence of the wavefront aberration to the transverse aberration. Stopping down shrinks the aberration blur rapidly, but the diffraction blur grows in proportion to the f-number.

optical-design-038.question: With the lenses unchanged, only the position of the aperture stop is moved along the axis. Which combination of aberrations remains unchanged? (Consider third-order aberrations.)
choices: Spherical aberration and axial colour, because the part of the lens crossed by the beam from an on-axis point does not depend on the stop position
Coma and astigmatism, because the part of the lens crossed by the beam from an off-axis point stays the same wherever the stop is placed
Distortion and lateral colour, because the chief ray's image height is set only by the lens's focal length and is not affected by the stop position
optical-design-038.explanation: The beam from an on-axis point passes through the same part of the lens wherever the stop is placed (provided the stop diameter is adjusted to keep the same beam size). Spherical aberration and axial colour therefore do not change with stop position, and neither does the field curvature set by the Petzval sum. Off-axis beams, however, cross different parts of the lens as the stop moves, and the path of the chief ray changes, so coma, astigmatism, distortion and lateral colour all change. Distortion, a shift in the image height of the chief ray, depends strongly on the stop position: even for a single lens, a stop in front gives barrel distortion and a stop behind gives pincushion distortion. Designers use the stop position as one of the variables for balancing aberrations.

optical-design-039.question: How does the diffraction image of a system whose aperture centre is blocked by a secondary mirror (a central obstruction), as in a Cassegrain telescope, compare with that of an unobstructed system of the same aperture? (Assume no aberrations.)
choices: The obstruction reduces the open aperture area, so the central peak broadens in proportion to it and the MTF cut-off frequency is lowered as well
The obstruction only reduces the amount of light; the shape of the point image and of the MTF is exactly the same as without it
The central peak becomes slightly narrower, but part of the energy moves into the surrounding rings and the MTF drops at mid spatial frequencies
optical-design-039.explanation: The diffraction pattern of an annular aperture is the amplitude pattern of the outer circle minus that of the inner circle. The central peak becomes slightly narrower, while the first and outer rings brighten, so a smaller fraction of the energy falls in the central peak. The MTF is the autocorrelation of the pupil, so removing its centre reduces the overlap at mid spatial frequencies and lowers the contrast there, but the cut-off frequency, set by the outer diameter, is unchanged. The width of the point image is governed by the outer diameter, so a broader central peak is the opposite of what happens. Nor does the obstruction merely dim the image: the larger the obstructed fraction, the more prominent the rings and the lower the image contrast.

optical-design-040.question: A lens design with an RMS wavefront error of λ/14 (Strehl ratio about 0.82) is scaled up by a factor of two in every dimension, keeping its shape and f-number (the focal length also doubles, and it is used at the same wavelength). Which value is closest to the Strehl ratio of the scaled lens? (Use the Maréchal approximation S ≈ exp[−(2πσ/λ)²], where σ is the RMS wavefront error.)
choices: About 0.45
About 0.82
About 0.67
optical-design-040.explanation: When every dimension is doubled, geometric aberrations double as lengths, and the wavefront error, a difference in optical path, doubles to λ/7. Then S ≈ exp[−(2π/7)²] = exp(−0.806) ≈ 0.45. About 0.82 assumes that the aberration relative to the wavelength does not change on scaling, but the wavelength is not scaled, so the aberration in waves doubles. About 0.67 takes the error as growing by √2, giving S ≈ 0.82², which applies the rule for adding independent errors in quadrature. At the same f-number the diffraction spot size is unchanged, so scaling a design up tends to push it away from the diffraction limit, and larger lenses need tighter correction.

optical-design-041.question: In endoscopes and periscopes that relay an image over a long distance with many sets of relay lenses, a field lens is placed near the position of each intermediate image. Which correctly describes the function of this lens?
choices: It gathers light at the intermediate image to brighten the image and also raises the magnification about twofold, widening the field that can be relayed
At the intermediate image it blocks light coming from outside the field, sharpening the edge of the imaged area and reducing stray light from the surroundings
Since ray heights do not change at the intermediate image, it steers the off-axis bundles into the next lens while keeping the magnification nearly unchanged
optical-design-041.explanation: At a lens located at an intermediate image, ray heights equal the image height itself, so placing a lens there hardly changes the image size or position. The ray directions, however, are bent, so off-axis bundles that would otherwise spread outward can be redirected into the aperture of the next relay lens. Without it, peripheral bundles would be clipped by the edge of the next lens, darkening the edge of the field and narrowing the field of view. In other words, the field lens images the pupil of the previous lens onto the next lens, linking the pupils. It does not increase magnification, and the only brightness gain is the reduced vignetting at the periphery. Defining the edge of the field and blocking light is the job of a field stop, not of a field lens.

optical-design-042.question: A surface deviates from its ideal shape by at most λ/10 (peak-to-valley, measured at 633 nm). Which pair correctly gives the wavefront error of the transmitted or reflected light if this surface is used as a plane mirror at normal incidence, and if it is used as one surface of a lens of index 1.5 (an air boundary, near-normal incidence)?
choices: λ/10 for the mirror and λ/10 for the lens surface, because the surface error becomes the wavefront error directly
λ/5 for the mirror and λ/20 for the lens surface, so the same surface error affects a mirror four times as much
λ/20 for the mirror and λ/5 for the lens surface, because refraction magnifies surface errors more strongly
optical-design-042.explanation: For a mirror, a surface displaced by a height h changes the round-trip path of the light by that amount on both the way in and the way out, so the wavefront error is 2h; a λ/10 surface error becomes a λ/5 wavefront error. For a refracting surface, the light passes through a height h of air instead of glass, and the optical path difference is (n − 1)h = 0.5h, giving λ/20. Therefore, for surfaces of the same accuracy, a mirror is affected 2/0.5 = 4 times as much as a refracting surface, which is why telescope primary mirrors and interferometer reference mirrors require tighter surface accuracy than lenses. The option in which the surface error becomes the wavefront error directly ignores the round trip in reflection and the index difference. The option that swaps the mirror and lens values has the sizes reversed.

optical-design-043.question: The Cooke triplet, three singlet lenses (positive, negative, positive) separated by air spaces, is known as a basic form of photographic lens. Why can it correct the main monochromatic and chromatic aberrations together with as few as three lenses?
choices: It has eight degrees of freedom, six surface curvatures and two spacings, which is enough to fix the focal length and correct the five Seidel aberrations and two chromatic aberrations
The three lenses handle the three primary colors red, green and blue separately, each bringing one color to focus so that the colors overlap on the image plane
The two outer positive lenses have the same shape, so their aberrations cancel automatically, while the central negative lens handles only spherical aberration and the stop controls the others
optical-design-043.explanation: Aberration correction is considered in terms of whether the number of quantities that can be freely varied in the design (degrees of freedom) is at least the number of conditions to be met. Besides the condition fixing the focal length, there are the five Seidel aberrations (spherical, coma, astigmatism, field curvature, distortion) and two chromatic aberrations, axial and lateral, making eight. The Cooke triplet has eight degrees of freedom in its six surface curvatures and two air spaces, and with the choice of glasses it is the simplest configuration that can just control them. Placing the negative lens in the middle, separated from the positive lenses, reduces the Petzval sum and flattens the field. The three lenses do not share the three colors. Even if the outer lenses have the same shape, the aberrations do not vanish automatically, and the negative lens takes part in correcting more than spherical aberration.

optical-design-044.question: In a camera zoom lens, the position of the in-focus image plane hardly moves when the focal length is changed. Which is the usual mechanism that achieves this?
choices: The refractive index of one lens group is changed by a voltage to change the focal length, so the magnification changes without moving any lens along the axis and the image plane stays put
Moving the group that changes magnification (the variator) shifts the image plane, so another group (the compensator) is moved in a fixed relation to cancel the shift
It uses the property that changing the aperture size also changes the focal length, varying the field of view in step with the aperture, so the image plane stays fixed
optical-design-044.explanation: Moving the main group that changes the focal length (the variator) along the axis changes the focal length of the system and at the same time shifts the position where the image forms. Therefore another group (the compensator) is moved simultaneously, in a fixed nonlinear relation set by a cam or similar, to keep the image plane in place. A lens that stays in focus while its focal length is changed in this way is called a zoom lens, as distinguished from a varifocal lens, which must be refocused. Liquid lenses whose index is changed by voltage exist, but they are not the mechanism of ordinary zoom lenses. The aperture size changes only brightness and depth of field, not the focal length or field of view.

optical-design-045.question: A camera lens consists of six singlet lenses spaced apart in air. If each air-glass surface (12 surfaces) has a reflectance of 4% without an antireflection coating and 0.5% with one, which pair is closest to the transmittance of the whole lens? (Ignore absorption and multiple reflections.)
choices: About 52% uncoated and about 94% coated
About 78% uncoated and about 97% coated
About 61% uncoated and about 94% coated
optical-design-045.explanation: Each surface transmits a fraction (1 − R), so for 12 surfaces the transmittance is 0.96¹² ≈ 0.61 uncoated and 0.995¹² ≈ 0.94 coated. About 52% estimates the loss by addition, 1 − 12 × 0.04, and the difference from multiplication grows when the reflectance is large. About 78% and about 97% count the six lenses as six surfaces, but each lens has two surfaces facing air. Reflected light is not only lost; it bounces between surfaces and reaches the image plane as ghosts and flare, lowering contrast. With 12 surfaces there are 66 pairs of surfaces that can produce a double reflection, and antireflection coatings greatly reduce this stray light as well. Zoom lenses with many elements became practical thanks to multilayer antireflection coatings.
